evidence.excerpt: Classification thresholds are routinely left at the default 0.5 in many applied clinical studies despite well-established evidence that asymmetric misclassification costs make this choice suboptimal. This paper reviews threshold selection methods including cost-minimisation, F-beta maximisation, utility-maximisation, and the Youden index, and provides an empirical comparison across twelve publicly deposited and in-house clinical tabular datasets ranging from 500 to 28,000 samples. Datasets cover six disease areas including cardiovascular risk, diabetes complications, and haematological malignancy. The comparison uses nested cross-validation to avoid threshold selection bias. Results show that cost-minimisation and F-beta methods are broadly equivalent when cost ratios are specified accurately, but that the Youden index consistently underperforms in high-imbalance settings with imbalance ratios above 1:15. The paper also provides guidance on eliciting cost ratios from clinical stakeholders and documents a structured interview protocol used with six clinicians at a teaching hospital in Novi Sad.
